# Who Is Andrea Soros? All About George Soros' Daughter

**Andrea Soros** is an American philanthropist and the daughter of investor and Open Society Foundations founder George Soros. Known professionally as Andrea Soros Colombel, she has supported education, Tibetan cultural preservation, and efforts to address poverty through charitable organizations. Her career has an independent record that extends well beyond her father's public profile. Her family background helps explain the attention she receives, but her work with Trace Foundation, Acumen, and other nonprofits is the more substantial part of her public biography.

Andrea Soros Colombel is the daughter of billionaire investor George Soros and Annaliese Witschak. An American philanthropist, she founded Trace Foundation in 1993, helped establish Acumen, and serves on the Open Society Foundations board. She is married to Eric Colombel, whose work with Tsadra Foundation also focuses on Tibetan traditions.

## Who Is Andrea Soros Colombel?

Andrea E. Soros Colombel is a foundation founder, nonprofit board member, and longtime supporter of international development. She established Trace Foundation in 1993 after spending time on the Tibetan Plateau, where she traveled and taught English. She also helped launch Acumen, an organization that invests in businesses addressing poverty, and has served on the board of Open Society Foundations.

Her interests range from Tibetan literature to environmental policy and nonprofit governance. Her public career involves supporting institutions rather than pursuing the financial trading work for which her father is famous. Organizational records commonly use her married surname, Colombel.

## Her Parents and the Soros Family

Andrea is the daughter of George Soros and his first wife, Annaliese Witschak. According to [CNN's biographical account of George Soros](https://www.kq2.com/cnn/cnn-world/2026/07/31/george-soros-fast-facts/), the couple had three children: Robert, Andrea, and Jonathan. George later had two more sons, Gregory and Alexander, with his second wife, Susan Weber. That makes Robert and Jonathan Andrea's full brothers, while Gregory and Alexander are her half-brothers.

George Soros, whose Hungarian birth name is György Soros, made his fortune in investment management before becoming widely known for philanthropy. He founded the Open Society Foundations, which support organizations working on rights, equity, justice, and democratic participation. Andrea's involvement with that network is a documented professional role, not simply an informal association based on their relationship.

Her brother Alexander Soros, often called Alex, is the current chair of Open Society Foundations. Andrea is also listed on its board of directors. The two therefore participate in the same institution, although their leadership titles and public responsibilities are different. Describing Andrea as the person who succeeded her father would be inaccurate.

## Andrea Soros' Age and Education

Official [UK Companies House records](https://find-and-update.company-information.service.gov.uk/officers/Yi823OI1SY58fHL8W6hc7LA9MlQ/appointments) give Andrea's birth month and year as June 1965. She was therefore 61 years old as of November 2026. This government filing supports the month and year without requiring a more specific birthday than the record itself provides.

She earned a bachelor's degree in literature, with honors, from the University of Chicago. She later received a graduate certificate from the Bard Center for Environmental Policy. Acumen's official biography confirms both credentials, which connect two recurring elements of her subsequent work: an interest in culture and concern for environmental sustainability.

## Founding Trace Foundation and Supporting Tibetan Communities

Trace Foundation is the organization most closely associated with Andrea's independent career. She founded it in 1993 following experiences as a traveler and English teacher on the Tibetan Plateau. The foundation's original purpose was to support Tibetan communities, particularly in areas within China, while respecting their culture and capacity to define local priorities.

Its early work combined grants for institutions and individuals with projects in education, health, rural development, and cultural preservation. [Trace Foundation's official history](https://www.trace.org/about) reports that it awarded more than 300 grants totaling nearly $14 million during its first decade. In 1995, it responded to severe winter conditions in western Sichuan, an early example of its involvement in local needs beyond cultural programming.

Over time, the organization expanded from grantmaking into directly implementing projects. It supported educational opportunity, vocational skills, and access to resources while emphasizing participation by local communities. Its stated approach linked practical improvements in living standards with the preservation of language and cultural identity, rather than treating those goals as competing priorities.

A particularly enduring initiative was Latse Library, established in New York City in 2003 as a center for contemporary Tibetan studies. Its collections and programming created a resource for Tibetan literature, culture, and scholarship outside the region. The project eventually developed into a separate nonprofit organization.

In October 2018, Andrea [announced that Trace would wind down](https://www.trace.org/to-the-many-friends-of-trace-foundation.html) most activities and come to a close. She explained that changing conditions had made direct work with communities on the Tibetan Plateau increasingly difficult. This matters when reading older biographies: descriptions of Trace as an expanding, fully operating foundation reflect its earlier history, not necessarily its present activities.

## Her Husband, Eric Colombel, and Tsadra Foundation

Andrea's husband is **Eric Colombel**, whose connection to her is confirmed by [Tsadra Foundation's own institutional history](https://www.tsadra.org/about-us/past-programs/). Eric established the organization around the beginning of the 2000s with Andrea's support. It was designed to help people in the West study, practice, and access the traditions of Tibetan Buddhism.

The foundation has supported translation, publication, contemplative practice, and higher education. Its history describes efforts to make important Tibetan texts available to new readers and to strengthen advanced study without interfering with established Buddhist communities. Andrea's involvement with Tsadra overlaps with her commitment to preserving Tibetan knowledge, but the organization has a distinct mission from Trace.

Their shared work does not establish Andrea's personal religious beliefs. Public biographies document charitable involvement rather than individual faith.

## Her Role at Acumen and Open Society Foundations

Andrea was a founding partner of Acumen in 2001, supporting its approach to tackling poverty through investment in entrepreneurs. She joined its board in 2005, served until 2014, and returned in 2017. In [announcing her return](https://acumen.org/news/andrea-soros-colombel-returns-to-acumens-board-of-directors/), Acumen credited her with helping develop its portfolio of off-grid energy companies.

She also serves on the board of Open Society Foundations. The organization's [official board listing](https://www.opensocietyfoundations.org/who-we-are/board-of-directors) currently names her alongside its chair, Alex Soros, and other board members. Her participation gives her a formal role in oversight at an institution founded by her father, while her work at Acumen remains a separate commitment.

Andrea's record includes work with organizations addressing sustainability and education. They also record a separate directorship at Systemiq Limited that ended in December 2021. The distinction is important: company records show specific legal appointments rather than a general claim that she currently directs both companies.

## Conclusion

Andrea Soros is George Soros' daughter, but her documented achievements stand on their own. She founded Trace Foundation to support Tibetan communities, helped build Acumen's work on poverty and energy access, and participates in the governance of Open Society Foundations. Her work with Eric Colombel on Tibetan cultural and educational initiatives adds another dimension to that record. Taken together, those contributions offer a more useful portrait than unsupported claims about her wealth or private family life.
